summary: Records, for historical interest, the EF design team's alternative proposal that the original RFC 2598 authors preferred but the working group did not adopt. It requires a bound on delay caused by other traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two groups argued over how to build a fast lane. This keeps the plan that lost, in case people are curious.

questions: how does delay bound measure delay
subtitle: An alternative definition of the Expedited Forwarding service, for the record

tldr.problem: The DiffServ working group had concerns about RFC 2598's definition of the Expedited Forwarding (EF) Per-Hop Behavior for prioritizing latency-sensitive traffic. A design team proposed an alternative based on delay bounds that the RFC 2598 authors preferred.
tldr.mechanism: The Delay Bound (DB) PHB specifies that for traffic not exceeding a configured rate, delay variation through a hop is strictly bounded by a formula: the maximum delay minus the minimum delay is at most S times the MTU divided by the arrival rate.
tldr.outcome: The working group adopted a different re-expression of EF (RFC 3246), but this document preserves the DB proposal for historical interest in case future implementers want to experiment with it.

today: RFC 3248 is an Informational document preserving the Delay Bound proposal for historical interest. The Expedited Forwarding PHB is defined by RFC 3246, which took a different approach. DB remains available for implementers who want to experiment with strict delay bounds as an alternative or complement to the adopted standard.

sections.title: The EF PHB Disagreement
sections.content: The Differentiated Services (DiffServ) working group is responsible for Per-Hop Behaviors (PHBs), which are rules routers follow to prioritize traffic. RFC 2598 defined the Expedited Forwarding (EF) PHB to provide a fast lane for delay-sensitive applications like voice. However, at the IETF meetings in 2000, the working group found concerns with the original RFC 2598 text. A volunteer 'EF Design Team' (the authors of this document) developed an alternative re-expression called Delay Bound (DB). Their proposal focused on guaranteeing strict bounds on how much other traffic can delay EF packets. The design team presented DB at the December 2000 IETF meeting, but the working group chose a different approach (RFC 3246). This document preserves the DB proposal for historical interest and potential future experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers building a fast-lane system disagreed on how to measure success. Team A said: 'Promise that packets will never be delayed by more than this much.' Team B won, so Team A's idea is here for reference.

sections.title: The Delay Bound Concept
sections.content: The Delay Bound PHB aims to strictly bound the delay variation caused by competing traffic. The core idea is simple: measure how long a packet would take to travel through a router if no other traffic competed with it (the 'ideal' time E(i)), then measure how long it actually takes with competing traffic present (D(i)). The DB PHB ensures D(i) minus E(i) never exceeds a specified bound: S times MTU divided by R, where R is the configured arrival rate and S is the router's scheduling score. This means a router promises not just that EF packets get priority, but that they will never be delayed more than a specific amount by any other traffic, regardless of congestion. Traffic MUST be policed and shaped at the network edge to maintain the rate limit R.
sections.plainLanguage: It's like promising: 'Your call will get through, and even if the network is busy, other traffic will hold up your call by at most this many milliseconds.'

sections.title: Implementation and Conformance
sections.content: A DB implementation does not need to conform over arbitrary parameter values. Instead, a router MUST specify the rates (R) and scores (S) for which it claims DB conformance, along with how much burstiness it can tolerate. The score S depends on the router's scheduler and is a characteristic of the device at a given rate R. Different implementations are free to exhibit different tolerance for bursts—some routers might handle sustained wire-rate packets well, others less so. The DB definition does NOT mandate a particular scheduling method; instead it defines parameters that bound the operating range. Network designers use these parameters to compare different DB implementations and decide which suits their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routers might be good at different speeds. Each router publishes its limits so network planners know what it can handle.

sections.title: Key Differences from Other Approaches
sections.content: The Delay Bound approach differs from other QoS models in several ways. First, the definition is explicit about competing traffic—it includes all DB traffic arriving on other ports and all non-DB traffic arriving anywhere on the router. Second, DB does not bound jitter (variability in inter-packet timing) but rather bounds delay variation relative to an ideal scenario. Third, the output rate is not specified; it is whatever is needed to meet the delay variation bound. Fourth, fragmentation is assumed to be avoided, not handled. When DB traffic passes through multiple routers, each hop must provide DB behavior for the bound to hold end-to-end. The RFC notes that DB packets MAY be remarked at domain boundaries only to other codepoints that satisfy DB, and tunneled DB traffic must remain marked as DB.
sections.plainLanguage: The Delay Bound idea says: 'I promise this level of interference, measured this specific way, under these conditions.' It's very precise about what is and is not guaranteed.

sections.title: Why It Lost and What Happened Instead
sections.content: At the December 2000 IETF meeting in San Diego, the DiffServ working group decided to pursue the alternative re-expression of EF that was developed by the RFC 2598 authors and clarified to also encompass the DB model. That work became RFC 3246, the standards-track definition of EF. The Delay Bound proposal is archived here for historical interest. Although the working group did not adopt it, the DB concept has merit for implementers who want strict delay bounds and may want to experiment with it in the future. The document suggests experimental DSCP value 101111 for DB traffic, but since this comes from the experimental code space, it may be reused by other proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: The group chose a different design, but wrote down the Delay Bound idea in case future engineers want to try it out.
